--- Page 1 ---
Layer-wise CPU-GPU Scheduling for LLM
Inference on Memory-Limited Consumer GPUs
Naoto Sugiura1, Yuta Tokusashi2, and Hiroki Matsutani1
1 Keio University, 3-14-1, Hiyoshi, Yokohama, Japan 223-8522
{nsugiura, matutani}@arc.ics.keio.ac.jp
2 SoftBank Corp., 1-7-1 Kaigan, Minato-ku, Tokyo, Japan, 105-7529
yuta.tokusashi@g.softbank.co.jp
Abstract. As large language model inference environments expand to-
ward consumer devices, it remains challenging to efficiently run models
that exceed GPU memory capacity in single-GPU settings. The latency
of transferring weights that do not fit in GPU memory accounts for about
98% of inference time and remains a major obstacle. In this paper, we
focus on the fact that during the decode phase, layer computation time
on the CPU can be shorter than weight transfer time, presenting an op-
portunity to hide weight transfers by utilizing this computation time.
Therefore, we propose a method to hide transfer latency by executing
certain layers on the CPU during the decode phase while asynchronously
transferring the next layer’s weights to the GPU in the background of
that computation. To realize this scheduling, we formulate the placement
of CPU/GPU computation and weight transfers as a latency minimiza-
tion problem and perform optimization using an approximation model
with relaxed temporal constraints. Evaluation results confirm that in a
consumer desktop environment, our approach accelerates OPT-30B in-
ference by 3.5× compared to HuggingFace Accelerate and 6.3× compared
to DeepSpeed Zero-Inference.
Keywords: Large language model · GPU · Scheduling.
1
Introduction
As the social implementation of large language models (LLMs) accelerates, the
environment for their inference is expanding from traditional, resource-rich cloud
infrastructures to resource-constrained consumer devices, such as smartphones
and personal computers (PCs). Market forecasts indicate that AI-powered PCs
will account for 54.7% of the PC market by 2026, while AI-powered desktops
are expected to reach a 42.1% share in the same year [2]. The growth of local
execution on PCs enables reduced response times and power consumption while
decreasing cloud dependency and enhancing data protection [2, 14]. Moreover,
another forecast suggests that the adoption of on-device AI, which does not rely
entirely on the cloud, will be driven primarily by privacy concerns [1]. Beyond
consumer PCs, LLMs are also anticipated to be integrated into fields such as
arXiv:2611.01393v1  [cs.DC]  1 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
2
N. Sugirua et al.
robotics [16] and autonomous driving [15]. Against this backdrop, LLM inference
on edge and consumer devices is becoming increasingly important.
LLMs are utilized in a wide range of applications, including document gen-
eration, summarization, translation, and coding assistance. In particular, local
inference on consumer devices is frequently employed for interactive applications,
such as chatbots, which generate responses by sequentially producing tokens for
each request. While some operational strategies aim for high throughput via
batching [8, 7], this paper primarily assumes a local interactive setting with low
concurrency. Key characteristics of this setting are that the effective batch size
tends to be 1 and that minimizing latency, which directly affects user experience,
is crucial [18].
However, LLM inference demands substantial computational resources and
memory capacity, presenting significant barriers to execution on resource-constrained
consumer devices. For instance, the OPT-30B [17] model requires over 60 GiB of
memory in FP16 format, which far exceeds the 32 GiB capacity of the RTX 5090,
a state-of-the-art consumer-grade GPU. When LLM weights cannot fit within
the GPU memory in a single-GPU environment, frameworks such as Hugging-
Face Accelerate [3] typically place weights in host memory and transfer them
to the GPU sequentially during computation. However, in this approach, weight
transfer time dominates the total latency. For example, when using OPT-30B,
transfer overhead accounts for approximately 98% of the total execution time
during the decoding phase, creating a severe performance bottleneck.
One direction for addressing this problem is model compression, such as
quantization [13]. However, some models still remain too large to fit in GPU
memory, and aggressive compression can degrade accuracy. Another direction is
offloaded inference, where weights and KV caches are placed on the host side.
Prior work has proposed methods that reduce transfer stalls through schedul-
ing that reuses weights across batches [8], as well as through overlapping data
transfers with computation and coordinating execution with the CPU [18, 7, 6].
FlexGen is based on a simple overlap between GPU computation and data trans-
fer, with only limited use of CPU computation [8]. As a result, prior work reports
that exposed PCIe transfer time still accounts for approximately 96–98% of the
total execution time [6]. Reducing latency in offloaded inference therefore hinges
on how effectively transfer time can be hidden. Park and Egger [7] hide transfers
by executing part of the intra-layer weights on the CPU and thereby accelerate
throughput-oriented inference, whereas our paper differs in that it targets the
reduction of exposed transfers during batch-size-1 decoding under offloading.
HeteGen exploits CPU-side computation through CPU-GPU tensor parallelism,
but its effectiveness depends on CPU computational capability. FlexInfer [6]
presents a framework that uses an estimator to select different execution policies
for prefill and decode, but its choices are limited to CPU-only execution, GPU
execution with transfers from host memory, and a static split called SplitGen, in
which only the portion of weights that fits on the GPU is executed on the GPU
and the remainder is executed on the CPU. It does not address the direction of
hiding transfers behind CPU computation.


--- Page 3 ---
A Layer-wise CPU-GPU LLM Scheduling for Consumer GPUs
3
In this paper, we propose layer placement and scheduling techniques to min-
imize exposed transfer time for offload inference in a single-GPU environment,
specifically targeting decoding with a batch size of 1. Our key observation is that
the per-layer computation time on the CPU may be shorter than the weight
transfer time during the decoding process. In this case, CPU computation is not
merely an alternative execution target but can serve as a planned computation
window for hiding transfers. Based on this observation, we assign each layer to
one of three modes: execution on the CPU, residency on the GPU, or placement
in host memory with transfer to the GPU at execution time followed by GPU
computation, which we call the stream mode. We then construct a latency model
based on the computation time and transfer time of each mode. We further intro-
duce an approximation model that relaxes the temporal constraints of transfers
and reduce the complex scheduling optimization to a ratio determination prob-
lem, thereby synthesizing an execution plan from offline measurements, namely
per-layer computation time and transfer time. At runtime, transfer for stream
execution blocks is hidden behind CPU computation blocks, thereby minimizing
inference latency.
In summary, this work offers the following contributions:
– We conduct an extensive analysis of LLM inference in consumer-grade desk-
top environments and quantitatively characterize the workload properties.
– We formulate the latency minimization problem for LLM inference in single-
GPU environments as an optimization problem involving the placement of
GPU residency, CPU computation, and stream computation.
– To accelerate LLM inference on consumer desktops, we propose a method
that minimizes latency by efficiently overlapping CPU computation with
weight transfers.
– Our evaluation demonstrates that for OPT-30B, the proposed method achieves
an inference speedup of 3.5× compared to Hugging Face Accelerate [3] and
6.3× compared to DeepSpeed ZeRO-Inference [4].
2
Background and motivation
2.1
LLM inference
LLMs are composed of multiple Transformer layers [11] and generate text by
repeatedly predicting the next token. This inference process can be broadly
divided into two stages, prefill and decode. First, the stage that processes the
entire input prompt at once is called prefill. In this stage, the Key and Value
tensors produced by the attention computation in each layer are accumulated as
a KV cache, and the first token is predicted. After that, the stage that generates
new tokens one by one while referring to and updating the KV cache is called
decode. Whereas prefill benefits from the parallel processing capability of GPUs,
decode is inherently sequential, and the latency of each step directly affects user-
perceived response time.
Within each layer, multi-head attention (MHA) and a multi-layer percep-
tron (MLP) are mainly executed in sequence. MHA is responsible for extracting

contextual information by combining Values according to the similarity between
Queries and Keys. In decode, the KV cache is reused to avoid recomputing past
Keys and Values, but the amount of memory access in attention increases as the
sequence length grows. The subsequent MLP applies two linear transformations
and an activation function to the output of attention, enabling more advanced
information transformation.
2.2
Performance analysis
In LLM inference, workload characteristics vary with runtime parameters such
as the phase and the input and output lengths. In this section, we analyze
the performance of LLM inference in a single-GPU setting where the model
weights do not fully fit in GPU memory. The hardware configuration follows
Section 5.1. In this paper, we assume batch size 1 as the primary use case for
LLM inference on consumer PCs. HuggingFace Accelerate [3] places the portion
of weights that fits in GPU memory on the GPU and keeps the remaining weights
in host memory, transferring them to the GPU on demand during execution.
In this approach, computation and transfer are serialized, so weight transfer
time directly contributes to end-to-end latency. As shown in Figure 1, transfers
account for most of the latency, indicating that host-to-GPU transfer becomes
the bottleneck when the full set of weights cannot reside in GPU memory on a
single GPU. During prefill, transfers account for 86–98% of the execution time for
OPT-30B. As the prompt length increases, the transfer fraction decreases, but it
remains substantial. During decode, transfers account for 98% of the execution

the same trend.
Because host-to-GPU transfers are slower than GPU computation, recent
work has proposed cooperative execution with CPU computation [7, 18, 6]. How-
ever, some studies primarily evaluate server-class CPUs equipped with matrix
extensions such as Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX). While some eval-
uations include environments with desktop CPUs, there are limited reports
that quantify the relationship among GPU computation, CPU computation,
and transfer time in the batch-size-1 decode setting that we primarily target.
Therefore, we conduct layer-level profiling in a consumer desktop environment.
Figure 2 and Figure 3 show per-layer computation times on the GPU and
CPU, respectively. For the CPU, we also report results across different thread
counts. Table 1 reports transfer time from host memory to GPU memory. Com-
paring GPU and CPU computation times, the GPU is more than 100× faster.
This gap is especially pronounced in the compute-intensive prefill phase, where
the GPU can be more than 1000× faster. Since prefill is compute-intensive,
CPU execution can be accelerated by increasing the number of threads. How-
ever, in many cases, CPU execution remains slower than the sum of transfer
time and GPU computation time, indicating that transferring weights to the


--- Page 6 ---
6
N. Sugirua et al.
GPU and computing there is more efficient than computing on the CPU. In
decode, increasing the thread count provides limited benefit. Nevertheless, com-
paring transfer time and CPU time shows that CPU computation is faster than
transfer in the decode phase. This indicates room for speedup by overlapping
CPU computation with transfers. OPT-66B has more parameters per layer than
OPT-30B, which increases latency, but the overall trends remain the same.
2.3
Motivation
GPUs accelerate LLM inference through their high matrix computation capa-
bility. However, in a single-GPU environment where all model weights cannot
reside in GPU memory, a practical design is to offload weights to host memory
and transfer them to the GPU on demand. In this setting, inference latency
is dominated by weight transfer time. As shown by the measurements in Sec-
tion 2.2, during decode, per-layer CPU computation time can be shorter than
weight transfer time, which suggests an opportunity to use CPU computation
as a planned computation window for hiding transfers.
However, to actually reduce exposed transfers, it is necessary to jointly de-
cide at the layer level which layers should be assigned to the CPU to create
hiding windows and when the weights of other layers should be transferred. As
discussed in Section 1, this design space has not been sufficiently explored in
prior work. In this paper, we aim to minimize the inference latency of one de-
code step by selecting, for each layer, among CPU execution, GPU residency,
and transferred GPU execution, and by using the layers executed on the CPU
as hiding intervals for weight transfers. However, how to optimally assign these
placements to individual layers is not straightforward.
3
Problem formulation
3.1
Analytical model
In a single LLM decode step (one-token generation), each layer i ∈{1, . . . , N}
is executed serially. We formulate the latency by focusing on the fact that each
layer can adopt one of the following three execution modes.
– cpu: Execute on the CPU. The computation time of layer i is ci.
– resident: Execute on the GPU, and the weights are resident on the GPU.
The computation time of layer i is gi, and no weight transfer is required.
– stream: Execute on the GPU, but the weights are transferred on demand.
The computation time of layer i is gi, and a transfer time wi is required.
The latency is determined once the execution mode mi ∈{cpu, resident, stream}
is selected for each layer. Since both resident and stream modes utilize the GPU
for computation, we define an indicator variable ui that represents whether layer
i is computed on the GPU as ui = 1[mi̸ = cpu]. Because the layers are processed
serially, the total latency L for one decode step is expressed as the sum of the
following four terms.


--- Page 7 ---
A Layer-wise CPU-GPU LLM Scheduling for Consumer GPUs
7
1. Total computation time of layers executed on the CPU: Tcpu(m) = PN
i=1(1−
ui)ci
2. Total computation time of layers executed on the GPU: Tgpu(m) = PN
i=1 uigi
3. Exposed transfer time (stall): Weight transfers for stream layers can proceed
in parallel with computation, but any portion that cannot be fully hidden
by computation appears as waiting time. We define this as Tstall(m) ≥0.
4. Activation transfer (CPU-GPU switching): Each time the execution device
switches between adjacent layers, an activation transfer cost a is incurred.
Let the number of switches be B(m) = PN−1
i=1 |ui−ui+1|, then the activation
transfer time is aB(m).
Based on these components, the latency L for a single decode step is repre-
sented by the following equation.
L(m) = Tcpu(m) + Tgpu(m) + Tstall(m) + aB(m)
(1)
The objective of this paper is to select m to minimize L(m) while satisfying the
GPU memory capacity constraints.
3.2
Approximation via transfer-computation balancing
The stall term Tstall(m) depends on detailed temporal conditions, including when
each transfer starts, which computation interval it overlaps with, and whether
the transfer finishes before the corresponding layer is executed. Directly mod-
eling these conditions leads to a complicated analysis. Therefore, rather than
tracking the fine-grained timing of each individual transfer, we introduce an ap-
proximation model that focuses on the relation between the total time required
for transfers and the total amount of computation time available to hide them.
In this approximation, transfers are treated as if they can be flexibly assigned
across computation intervals, and the individual deadline constraints of each
transfer are relaxed. Under this approximation, the stall term is interpreted as
the portion of the total transfer time that remains exposed even after overlap
with computation. We also assume that CPU computation and weight transfer
to the GPU can proceed independently and can fully overlap.
First, the total transfer time required for layers executed in stream mode
is expressed as W(m) = PN
i=1[mi = stream] wi. Similarly, the total amount of
computation time that can potentially hide transfers is expressed as C(m) =
Tcpu(m) + Tgpu(m). In the approximation model, we assume that the exposed
stall is the portion of the total transfer time W(m) that cannot be hidden within
the computation time C(m), which yields
Tstall(m) ≈max(0, W(m) −C(m)).
(2)
Furthermore, since a is sufficiently small compared with the other terms, we
ignore it in the following analysis. In our experimental environment, a is only
0.005 ms. The latency in the previous subsection can then be approximated as
L(m) ≈C(m) + max(0, W(m) −C(m))
= max(C(m), W(m)).
(3)

That is, the latency is determined by whichever is larger, the total computation
time C(m) or the total transfer time W(m). In general, in offloaded inference
on a single GPU, transfer time is much larger than computation time, that is,
wi ≫gi. Therefore, in the standard approach that executes all layers on the
GPU, we typically have W(m) > C(m), and transfer becomes the bottleneck.
To mitigate this bottleneck, it is effective to intentionally increase C(m) by
executing some layers on the slower CPU, thereby hiding the transfer cost of the
remaining stream layers within that computation time.
Based on this idea, we next consider the optimal execution block while re-
specting the GPU memory capacity limit. To efficiently overlap CPU compu-
tation with weight transfer, it is desirable to form an execution block in which
the weights of y stream layers are transferred asynchronously to the GPU while
x layers are computed on the CPU. If the computation time is approximately
uniform across layers, the increase in total computation time caused by assigning
a layer to the CPU can be approximated by the average ¯
∆= E[ci −gi] and the
increase in total transfer time caused by assigning a layer to stream mode can
be approximated by the average ¯w = E[wi]. Here, the GPU computation time gi
is much smaller than both the CPU computation time ci and the transfer time
wi, that is, gi ≪ci, wi. Thus, in practice, we can approximate C(m) ≈Tcpu(m).
Moreover, we have
¯
∆≈E[ci] = ¯c. Under these approximations, minimizing
max(C(m), W(m)) becomes equivalent to balancing Tcpu(m) and W(m). Hence,
a desirable ratio satisfies ¯cx ≈¯wy. Therefore, under the integer constraint, we
solve
min
x,y∈Z |¯c x −¯w y|
(4)
and use the resulting ratio x : y to allocate non-resident layers between cpu and
stream modes.
4
Proposed method
In this section, we describe how to construct an execution plan based on the
formulation in Section 3 and how to run inference accordingly. Figure 4 provides
an overview. First, our method obtains per-layer CPU computation time and
transfer time via offline profiling. Then, it determines the execution mode for
each layer, and the inference module runs inference following the resulting plan.

4.1
Execution plan construction
We next construct the execution plan by assigning each layer to resident, CPU, or
stream execution. To obtain x and y that satisfy Eq. 4, the average computation
time per layer ¯c and the average transfer time per layer ¯w are required. In
our method, we use values collected through offline profiling to compute the
numbers of layers x and y that form the optimal execution block. Using these
profiled values, Algorithm 1 performs a continued-fraction search to find integer
values of x and y that minimize |¯cx −¯wy| under the constraint x + y ≤N.
Next, we determine the number of resident layers, denoted by nresident. Let
K be the effective GPU memory capacity, that is, the maximum number of
layers that can be used for weight placement after excluding the space required
for the KV cache and temporary activation buffers. In the inference process of
our method, an additional temporary space is required to transfer and retain
the weights of y layers as a batch, which we call the stream buffer. Therefore,
to maximize the number of resident layers while satisfying the GPU memory
capacity constraint, nresident is uniquely determined as nresident = K −y, which
is obtained by subtracting the y layers reserved for the stream buffer from the
effective capacity K.
Among the total N layers, the remaining N −nresident layers that cannot
reside on the GPU are partitioned into blocks with the computed ratio of x
to y. At runtime, these blocks are scheduled so that CPU computation and
stream execution are processed alternately and in parallel. As shown in Figure 5,
this reduces inference latency compared with an on-demand loading scheme. As
a result, the method fully utilizes precious GPU memory for resident layers
while using only the minimum required stream buffer, enabling inference that
completely hides transfer latency.
4.2
Inference procedure
We then describe how inference is executed under this plan. At runtime, the
resident layers are first transferred to the GPU. During inference, layers are
processed in order, and each layer is executed on either the CPU or the GPU
according to the plan. For stream layers that are executed on the GPU, asyn-
chronous transfer is initiated immediately before the computation of the first
CPU layer in the execution block. At this point, the transfer proceeds in parallel
with the computation of the CPU layers. After the transfer completes, the loca-
tion of the weights referenced by the corresponding layer is switched to the GPU
side, and the computation is performed when that layer is reached. Activations

are moved to the required device only when the computation device changes
between adjacent layers.
In prefill, the KV cache for past tokens does not yet exist, so auxiliary inputs
such as positional information and attention masks are prepared only once at
the beginning of the forward pass and then reused across layers. This reuse is
possible because these auxiliary inputs do not change across layers for the same
input sequence, and it avoids the cost of regenerating them for each layer. As
shown by the analysis in Section 2.2, CPU computation is slower in the prefill
phase, so transferring the weights to the GPU and executing there is faster.
Therefore, in the prefill phase, even layers assigned to the CPU are transferred
to the GPU and executed there.
In decode, tokens are generated one by one while retaining the KV cache for
past tokens. Since the plan divides layers between the CPU and the GPU, the KV
cache is also placed according to the execution device of each layer. Specifically,


--- Page 11 ---
A Layer-wise CPU-GPU LLM Scheduling for Consumer GPUs
11
The KV cache of CPU-executed layers is placed on the host side, while that of all
other layers is placed on the GPU. With FP16 and batch size 1, the maximum
KV cache size per layer is 56 MiB for OPT-30B and 72 MiB for OPT-66B, so
its memory impact is small compared with that of the weights. After that, the
layers are processed sequentially at each step, and inference proceeds in the same
manner while inserting transfers of weights and activations when needed. At each
step, the completion of weight transfers and computation is synchronized with
CUDA events, which preserves the dependencies among transfer, computation,
switching of weight references, and reuse of temporary buffers.
4.3
Implementation details
Our method is implemented on top of HuggingFace Transformers [12]. To min-
imize transfer latency, we use pinned memory. The weights of stream-targeted
layers are packed into contiguous memory regions and kept on the host side in
page-locked memory. These weights are then transferred asynchronously to a
temporary buffer on the GPU, after which the storage location of the weights
referenced by the target layer is switched to the GPU side and computation is
performed. After computation, the reference is switched back to the host side,
and the temporary buffer on the GPU is overwritten and reused. Therefore, along
this path, no weight transfer is performed from the GPU back to the host.
5
Evaluation
5.1
Setup
Because our method does not use compression or approximation and therefore
causes no accuracy degradation, we evaluate only performance. As performance
metrics, we use end-to-end latency and energy consumption. The evaluation is
conducted on a system equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 5090 with 32 GiB of
memory and an Intel Core Ultra 7 265F @ 2.40 GHz with 128 GiB of memory.
The GPU and the host are connected via PCIe Gen5 ×16. Experiments are
conducted using NVIDIA CUDA 12.4.131. CPU computation is configured to
use 8 threads. Although the Core Ultra 7 includes an NPU, it is not used in this
paper. We use OPT-30B and OPT-66B [17] and Llama2-70B [10] as the target
models. FP16 is used as the data type. We evaluate the models with prompt
lengths of 256 and 1024, while fixing the decode length to 32. As baselines, we use
Hugging Face Accelerate [3], DeepSpeed Zero-Inference [4], and two policies from
FlexInfer, namely CPU-only and SplitGen. CPU-only executes all computation
on the CPU. SplitGen executes the portion of weights that fit in GPU memory
on the GPU, while executing the remaining portion on the CPU.
5.2
Inference performance
Figure 6 shows the end-to-end latency of each method for OPT-30B, OPT-66B,
and Llama2-70B with prompt lengths of 256 and 1024. For OPT-30B with a 256-
token prompt, the proposed method is 3.5×, 6.3×, 2.8×, and 1.5× faster than

Fig. 6: End-to-end latency comparison with prompt lengths of 256 and 1024.
DeepSpeed is omitted for OPT-66B and Llama2-70B because of out of memory.
Accelerate, DeepSpeed, CPU-only, and SplitGen, respectively. For OPT-66B, the
proposed method is 3.5× faster than Accelerate, 6.1× faster than CPU-only, and
1.4× faster than SplitGen. For Llama2-70B, the proposed method incurs 22%
higher latency than SplitGen when the prompt length is 256. This is because
Llama2-70B itself is large, and pinned memory further increases pressure on host
memory. On-demand loading methods such as Accelerate and DeepSpeed process
all layers on the GPU, so latency varies little with changes in prompt length. Sim-
ilarly, because the proposed method also uses on-demand loading for the prefill
stage, the difference in latency due to prompt length is small. In contrast, CPU-
only and SplitGen perform the prefill on the CPU, which leads to a significant
difference based on prompt length. In the CPU-only method, latency increases
as the model size grows because the computational load increases. While transfer
time is a major bottleneck for Accelerate and DeepSpeed, the proposed method
achieves higher speeds by utilizing CPU computational resources and performing
computation in parallel with data transfer.

Fig. 7: Breakdown of
execution time. Tx de-
notes transfer.
Figure 7 shows the execution time breakdown of the
proposed method with a 256-token prompt. For OPT-
30B and OPT-66B, the ratio of exposed transfers is min-
imal, as 99.6% and 99.8% of the transfers are hidden by
computation, respectively. In contrast, almost all trans-
fers are exposed for Llama2-70B. The plan is made us-
ing average computation and transfer times. However,
host memory pressure makes these times unstable, so
the execution does not follow the plan as expected. A
potential countermeasure is to adopt worst-case mea-
surements during the profiling phase. The major overhead of our method is
execution plan construction. However, this takes only 3.2 seconds, and because
the plan is reusable, its impact on overall performance is negligible.

A Layer-wise CPU-GPU LLM Scheduling for Consumer GPUs
13
prompt and 32-token output. The proposed method achieves the lowest total en-
ergy consumption, outperforming DeepSpeed, Accelerate, CPU-only, and Split-
Gen by 4.9×, 3.1×, 4.6×, and 2.7×, respectively, primarily due to its shorter
inference time. The proposed method and SplitGen, both of which perform com-
putation on both the CPU and GPU, exhibit higher average power consumption,
at 273 W and 262 W, respectively. In contrast, the average power consumption
is 219 W for Accelerate, 199 W for DeepSpeed, and 193 W for CPU-only. How-
ever, because DeepSpeed and CPU-only have longer execution times, their total
energy consumption is higher.
6
Related work
FlexGen [8] proposes a zig-zag scheduling that reuses weights across batches to
maximize throughput. Park and Egger [7] reduce single-layer latency by using
dynamic programming to split each layer into three segments, with the first and
third executed on the CPU and the second on the GPU. These approaches target
batch-oriented workloads and focus on throughput-oriented inference accelera-
tion. HeteGen [18] overlaps CPU computation, transfer, and GPU computation
through heterogeneous tensor parallelism, but relies on substantial CPU com-
pute capability. FlexInfer [6] adapts execution to runtime conditions by choosing
among CPU-only, on-demand GPU execution, and SplitGen, but does not use
CPU execution as a transfer-hiding window. Relatedly, KVPR [5] and Shad-
owKV [9] target KV-cache offloading for long-context inference. In contrast, our
work targets batch size 1 decode with weight offloading and minimizes exposed
transfer time through layer-wise placement into CPU, resident GPU, and stream
modes.
7
Conclusion
In this paper, we aimed to minimize LLM inference latency in resource-constrained
single-GPU environments and proposed an optimization method for placing
GPU computation, CPU computation, and stream-based computation. In con-
ventional offloading methods, weight transfer over PCIe has been a bottleneck.
Our method addresses this issue by executing some layers on the CPU and asyn-
chronously transferring weights during that computation time, thereby realizing
execution blocks that hide transfer latency. Our evaluation on a consumer desk-
top equipped with an RTX 5090 showed that, for OPT-30B, our method achieved
a 3.5× speedup and 3.1× lower energy consumption than HuggingFace Accel-
erate. These results indicate that our method is effective for the growing use of
personal-use LLM inference in resource-constrained single-GPU environments.
